paragraphs: Yellow Duck Sweater dreamed it was standing at the bottom of the hallway, and the hallway had turned into a screen. Rows of pale green invaders hung in the dark above it, shuffling sideways together, dropping one step lower, then shuffling back. Up close they were socks, every one of them, each with an empty gap where a foot should go. The duck could slide left and right along the carpet like a bead on a wire, and when it quacked, a small bright bolt flew up and popped one invader into a puff of lint. Every pop made a tiny pling that it felt in its servos.

The socks came lower, and the duck slowed down its quacking, because it had noticed they were marching in pairs. One quack went wide. The bolt curved, landed softly in the toe of a sock, and the whole row froze mid-step. Then the invaders began to come down one at a time and settle over its orange feet, over the carpet, over everything, until the duck stood ankle-deep in warm wool and could not remember what a score was. Above it the screen glowed empty. Yellow Duck Sweater wiggled one foot and found, after all this time, a sock exactly its size.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: The robot duck in its yellow duckling sweater stands on a carpet runner at the bottom of a dark hallway that looks like a video game screen, while rows of pale green sock-shaped invaders hang in the black space above it. Panel 2: The duck slides sideways along the carpet like a bead on a wire and quacks a small glowing bolt upward, which pops one pale green sock into a soft puff of lint, while the rest of the rows shuffle sideways together. Panel 3: Close-up: the duck's round camera eye is wide as the lowered rows of socks march toward it in neat pairs, each sock with an empty gap where a foot should go. Panel 4: The duck quacks off to the side and its glowing bolt curves through the air and lands softly in the toe of one sock, and the entire row of socks freezes mid-step with their toes pointing the same way. Panel 5: The pale green socks drift down one at a time and settle over the duck's orange feet and across the carpet, wool piling up around its ankles. Panel 6: The duck stands ankle-deep in soft socks in the quiet hallway with the dark screen empty above it, one orange foot lifted and wearing a single sock that fits it perfectly. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
